utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik, IT-00-39-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Edgerton, I see you're standing. You're together with Mr. Hannis this morning and I see for the Defence there's Ms. Loukas and Ms. Cmeric. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no protective measures effective --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in respect of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Mehmed Music.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have received a Rule 90(F) summary. Has this been discussed with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've seen the Rule 89(F) summary. I can indicate that there is an additional issue that I wish to raise at this point, but it's not related to the 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would it be -- since I do not know what the issue is, would it be better to do it now or would it be better to do it once the witness has been called?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can indicate what it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yet again, we have the, as it were, running sore of the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The supplemental information sheet arrived Sunday afternoon. The witness has, of course, given four previous statements over the last 12 years, and now suddenly the witness indicates that he saw Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour, at a particular detention facility. Now, Your Honour, of course there's no provision for visits to the United Nations Detention Unit on a Sunday, so I have not, of course, consulted with my client in relation to this issue. I've asked Ms. Cmeric to give Mr. Krajisnik, which she has done this morning, the relevant supplemental information sheet. In those circumstances, I can indicate, Your Honour, that at the end of the evidence in chief, the Defence certainly will not be in a position to cross-examine this witness, in view of the very, very late and new information. So, Your Honour, I place that on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I submit there are potentially two alternatives, two alternatives being: Your Honours do not admit this evidence, and the matter proceeds on the basis of the material that has previously been indicated in relation to this witness; or, if Your Honours are minded to allow the Prosecution to elicit this evidence, well, in those circumstances, Your Honour, there are clearly -- there's a need for a conference and there's the need for further investigation, because the information also relates to another person, of course, who will need to be consulted. So in those circumstances, Your Honour, I think it's very clear in a the late arrival certainly places the Defence in a particularly invidious position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'd like to have your comment and I would like to add one question to the questions already raised by Ms. Loukas. We're dealing with an 89(F) witness, and I would say, as a general rule, we would not apply 89(F) -- to read out part of the written statement or the summary of the written statement, if the evidence as such would not qualify under 92 bis. The introduction of the accused at -- in one of the camps, well, would certainly put them in a quite different position from what is in general terms presented until now by the Prosecution where there was no direct presence of the accused in any detention facility, which I think in terms of acts and conduct of the accused might be a totally different matter. So, apart from the two suggestions Ms. Loukas made, I'd like to add this question, and, of course, a the same time I'm wondering what's happening. What's happening in my view is that at this moment the Prosecution is relying on information given by witnesses well in advance of the start of this trial, and perhaps even well in advance of the presence of the accused before this Tribunal. But then to wait until the very, very last day to update that information knowing that the testimony of this witness is going to be presented in this case, and to leave these very important matters up to the last Sunday before the witness arrives, I would think that at least preparatory work should be done in the field before so as to know what surprises could be expected. So that's also an issue I'd like you to briefly address if you're in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're awaiting -- Your Honour, while we're awaiting a response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. While we're awaiting a response, there appears to be a problem with the LiveNote transcript. It seems to have frozen on the computer screens. It seems to be running on the laptops but not on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even on the laptops, I see that it's not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No. It's stopped on the laptops as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we therefore meanwhile ask the assistance of the technicians to have the transcript running again. It gives the Prosecution some additional time to consider the answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just needed to consult with Mr. Hannis to see whether there were any policy issues involved here that I wasn't otherwise aware of. I think actually Your Honour is quite correct. These statements as you can see particularly in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, when the transcript is not -- no, when the transcript is not running, we should perhaps at all refrain from speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I will see whether the transcript is running again. It is not. It is not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it's now -- one second. I take it that now the transcript is updated because the transcriber has repaired the transcript. Yes. We're now there again. Is it also functioning on the laptops as it is on mine? Yes. Then, Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to continue: As you can see, particularly in this case, the statements are often taken years ago, and in the case of Mr. Music, years before the accused before this Trial Chamber was even a target. So at that point in time, and I being one of the interviewers, I'm in a position to say I did not ask the witness anything about any sightings of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Perhaps remiss of me at that time, and in fact it's quite correct that these witnesses, for different reasons, largely having to do with the completion strategy and budgetary constraints, a number of these witnesses are not seen again as part of the witness preparation until they're brought here by the victim witness unit. So, in fact, it's not a great justification, Your Honour. Your assessment of the situation is entirely accurate. I can only offer that yesterday, on seeing Mr. Music for the first time in a year, which is a year ago being the date I congratulated him after his having finished his testimony in the Milosevic case, he offered for the first time that he had seen Mr. Krajisnik and we simply did our utmost to disclose that information as soon as we heard it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still surprising that if Mr. Music was here one year ago, when it was known that he was on the witness list or at least we could expect him on the witness list, in this case, that no specific interview has been held with him in respect of the specifics of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to his testimony in the Milosevic case, I was not involved in that in terms of preparation or in any other regard, Your Honour, so I can't speak to that. And I wasn't specifically tasked at that time with any witness preparation for the Krajisnik case. I only went to see him because of my personal acquaintance with him. And perhaps I should indicate that, just a further consideration, that Mr. Music was previously a 92 bis witness. He was upgraded to viva voce witness, or in this case, 89(F) witness, because another Hadzici witness, Zijad Okic, had passed away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's quite some coincidence, because under 92 bis, he would not even have come to The Hague. You would have missed that information that you're presenting now anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just confer with the other Judges for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not received any of the supplementary information; therefore, at this moment to give decisions is to ask, I guess. Not admitting it would not be something to consider at this moment. But at the same time, the Chamber fully understands the need for further preparation for the cross-examination, even if that would involve a recall of the witness, which of course we always try to avoid. And therefore, I think the OTP is invited to see in one way or another -- I mean, it's not the first time that we have these surprises at such short notice. So therefore, for example, to see whether six or eight or ten weeks in advance, that at least there will be a brief interview by whoever it will be who acts on behalf of the OTP to see whether any further surprises are to be expected. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one suggestion I would make, of course, is that there is, in fact, not necessarily a need to wait until the witness arrives in The Hague to conduct some sort of preliminary interview. We do have the benefit of telephones, and it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm suggesting. When I was talking about six, eight, or ten weeks in advance, that it was -- whether it's by telephone, whether it's by any other means, by any investigator who would see whether there's any need for an update. That's what I suggested to the OTP right away, in order to that similar surprises will occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed shocks sometimes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one further thing, Your Honour. With respect to the information report, I can advise that I did e-mail the information report to Mr. Zahar and Mr. De Hemptinne yesterday, along with to the Defence counsel, so perhaps we could try and provide Your Honours with a copy of that report on the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, although the Chamber is aware of -- the Defence is aware of -- usually receives the written statements and just in preparation of the oral testimony, in this case, the Chamber prefers to hear any additional evidence orally to receive it in its direct form and not to first read at this moment the new information you have elicited from him. Therefore, at this moment, if you're ready to start the examination-in-chief of the witness, we'll ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Music. Do you hear me in a language you understand? I take it from your answer that you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Ms. Edgerton, counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Edgerton, before we start, could I ask your attention for paragraph 4 of what is presented to us as the 89(F) summary, paragraph 4, second line. It reads: "The witness could see." And then follows a number and then follows a qualification and then the word "around" appears. If you -- if the witness could see 50 or 60. And if you are summarising the statements of the witness, I think that it would be wise that if words as we find them in this line are used, that you clearly indicate that these are the words of the witness rather than anything else. So, therefore, it could have been read: The witness could see 50 or 60 people. He calls. That makes it, I take it, more neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if, before we go further, the witness could be given copies now of the four statements he's variously provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They have been presented. Have they been attributed an exhibit yet, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The B/C/S version will be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just in terms -- I don't know how Your Honour wishes to proceed in this regard. In terms of the numbering of the statements, the original versions of the 1993, 1994, and 1998 statements are in B/C/S; the original version of the 1997 statement is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The original language gets the number without a ".1". So that means that for the first statements, the English translation will get a ".1". As far as the 1997 statements are concerned, there the B/C/S version is the ".1" version. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, I see you have before you copies in your own language of four documents, one dating from 1993, one from 1994, one from 1997, and one from 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity recently to review those documents in detail?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise those documents?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are those documents copies of statements that you've given on four separate occasions to the Bosnian authorities and representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you reviewed those documents, did you find them to be true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: There were some corrections made in two places, I think, two or three places. There were printing mistakes, typing errors. And something that I added which I remembered later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to those corrections which you asked me to make on the record today, perhaps I could deal with them, and they both relate to the statement from 1997, English -- well, paragraph number 43. You wish to correct a place-name set out in the second-to-last line of paragraph 43. The place-name, which presently reads "Rastovica" you said should read "Rastelica"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the second correction, as I have noted here, appears in paragraph 76, the sentence which in English reads: "I never saw that group who had beaten us in the corridor again." I understand from you that the version in your language is missing the "G" at the beginning of the word "group." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You asked me to have those corrections made on the record?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, leaving aside for the moment the information which you remembered, which we'll deal with later, can you now confirm that these statements you have before you are copies of your statements, which are true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder, then, Your Honour, if I could ask these documents receive the appropriate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first document dated 18th of April, 1993, will then receive the reference P407/A. As it is a translation, it will have a dot 1. The second document, dated the same date, 18th of April, 1993, will receive the reference P407/A, as it is the original. The document dated 23rd of March, 1994 is a translation, will receive the P407/B.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I think we usually don't use the slashes, so let's just make it 407A and 407A.1. Now the same for P407B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for this. I then go to the document 23rd of March, 1994, receive the reference P407B, as it is the original. The document dated 26th of June, 1997, witness statement, will receive the reference P407C. The document dated the same date will receive the reference P407C.1, as it is a translation of the previous one. The document dated 21st of February, 1998 will receive the reference P407D.1, as it is a translation. The document dated the same date, 21st of February, 1998, will receive the reference P407D, as it is the original. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, with the Trial Chamber's permission, and Mr. Music's permission, I'd like to read in a summary of the evidence as set out in the statements which are now filed as Exhibit number -- collectively filed as Exhibit number 407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness, Mr. Mehmed Music, is a Muslim from Donji Hadzici, Hadzici municipality. Prior to the outbreak of war, he lived in the Muslim settlement of Musici. Around the beginning of March 1992, the witness was able to see Serbs in former JNA uniforms climbing the hills around a Serb village carrying guns and ammunition to the peaks around them. They were coming from a barracks in Blazuj. The Muslims were asked in late April 1992 to surrender their weapons. In early May, after the outbreak of hostilities in the region of Hadzici, bullets, dumdum bullets, tracers, and flares were fired into the village of Musici. From 15 May, shells were fired at the village. On 17 or 18 May, on two separate occasions, local Serbs again urged the Muslim villagers to surrender their weapons, the second time calling through a megaphone, saying they would burn the village if they failed to surrender. Villagers refused to surrender their weapons. The village was shelled that evening, and the shelling lasted for three days. Around noon on 20 May 1992, Serbs forces surrounded Musici and entered the village. They were supported by two anti-aircraft guns. The witness was in his house at the time with several others. Two local Serbs known to the witness, armed with automatic rifles and wearing former JNA uniforms entered the house and held those present at gunpoint. The witness believes these Serbs to have been members of the military police. 14 Muslim males from Musici, including the witness, were gathered in front of a house. The witness could see 50 or 60 people he calls Chetniks around. Outside the house, the witness saw the bodies of three males from Musici. One of the witness's brothers, Miralem, was among this group of 14 captured men. Their captors marched him around the settlement, calling people to surrender. The 14 men from Musici were taken under guard to the primary school in Hadzici, and from there to the garage of the Hadzici Municipal Assembly building. Interrogations of the detainees began immediately, taking place in the municipality building itself. The witness was detained in this garage for six days, during which time additional detainees were brought in, all Muslim. Eventually there came to be 47 people in this garage. On the third day of his detention, the witness was taken with the other men from Musici to load ammunition from the former -- pardon, me. From the JNA ammunition store in Zunovnica. Another group of detainees from the Hadzici KSIRC (culture, sports, and recreational centre) was brought there for the task. On the sixth day of his detention, the witness was taken with all but three of the men from Musici to the KSIRC. There were approximately 60 Muslim men there at that time, and one woman. The witness recognised the head of the detention facility in the KSIRC to be Momo Vujovic. He knew the guards as well. The witness saw detainees at the KSIRC beaten and mistreated. On the second day of Bajram, the witness saw people who were identified to him as Arkanovci come into the sports hall. They wore camouflage uniforms and gloves which had the fingertips cut off. Their faces were painted black. A woman was among this group, who the witness recognised as being from Ilidza. He saw her sexually abuse two of the male detainees, in one case ordering a prisoner to perform fellatio on another. The witness saw members of this group chase one Muslim male around the inside of the hall with a flag-pole. They beat him, as well as other prisoners who the witness knew. By 22 June, there came to be 282 detainees in the part of the sports hall where the witness was held, all male. On or around 22 June 1992, the detainees were transferred by bus to Kula prison. There, the buses were boarded by people who the witness describes as Chetniks, who beat the prisoners. After the beating, the buses went to the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks in Lukavica. All the men were taken from the buses and into the barracks building. All the way to the barracks and up a flight of stairs, the prisoners had to run a gauntlet of persons who the witness refers to as Chetniks, and were beaten as they ran. The prisoners were put into two rooms. The witness saw prisoners called out by name from the room for interrogations, returning beaten. They heard the screams of one prisoner and then a shot. This prisoner didn't return. These beatings lasted until about 3.00 a.m. The next morning, all of the 280 men were moved into one room at another part of the barracks. An army officer took a list and called out 48 names from among the detainees. The witness believed he heard his name called out as the 48th person. As he got to the door, he had to run slowly along a corridor through a zigzag gauntlet of men wearing red berets. He was brutally beaten and cursed. From the way the men in red berets spoke, the witness could tell they were not from there. Through the corridor, the witness came upon a man lying down, covered in blood. They told him to pick him up. He saw it was his brother, and carried him to the next room. In the next room, the witness saw the prisoners who will be called lined up against three walls, and in the middle of the room there was a desk with three Serb officers. They asked the witness who he was and the witness explained why he had come. The witness saw these men had a large list of people, and the names they had called out were circled in red. The witness was told his name was not on the list and to get out. He ran back through the gauntlet to what remained of the original group of detainees, beaten again. The witness has never seen any of the group of 47 men (including his brother) since that time. After some time, another group came in to beat the remaining prisoners. The prisoners were forced to sing Serb songs. The witness remained in Lukavica for three days, but the prisoners were still beaten when being taken to the toilet. On the third day, the witness and approximately 232 other detainees were taken by bus to Kula. At Kula, the prisoners were divided into two rooms. Conditions were cramped. There was poor sanitation. While detained at Kula, the witness was interrogated by a man named Predrag Ceranic. Eventually, the detainees were separated into several rooms with slightly better conditions. On 30 June 1992, all persons born before 1936 were ordered to leave. 75 detainees of the approximately 280 were immediately released at the Vrbanja bridge in Sarajevo. On 23 July 1992, the witness and five other men were called out and told they were going to be exchanged. An UNPROFOR vehicle came to pick them up. At Ilidza, the vehicle was stopped and the witness and one other detainee were told to step out. They were taken to a cell in the building of the Ilidza public security station. There were no windows in this cell. The witness was housed in this cell until 8th of September, 1992. The head of the station was Tihomir Glavas. During his detention at the Ilidza police station, one of the policeman told the witness they had three different forces there: National, city, and a special intervention force. The witness saw weekend Chetniks there who had come from Serbia and Montenegro. On 8th of September, following two abortive exchange attempts, the witness was transferred to the KSIRC, where there were 500 detainees, men, women, children, and elderly. Some ten days later, all women, children, and some of the elderly men were released so that out of 500 detainees, only 84 remained, including the witness. On 23 October, the witness and approximately 70 other detainees were transferred by bus from Hadzici to the Svrake camp. There were approximately 102 prisoners already there. The witness remained at Svrake until 5 November 1992. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. I take it you have additional questions to the witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, having read out this summary, I'd now like to ask you some questions, largely relating to clarifications or additional details based on the information contained in those four statements you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First, then, relating to the first paragraphs of these statements, you talk about your village of Musici and its location. At this time, I'd like to show you a map, which you prepared yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. And do you have a copy of the map, Mr. Registrar? If we could have this map marked with an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the exhibit number for this map will be P408. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On this map, you made some markings yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you've marked at point number 1 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Number 1 indicates my village in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just moving on further in your statements: In paragraph 7 and 8 of your statement to the Tribunal, you mention a camp called Catina Bara in Blazuj. Could you point out, or have you been able to point out the location called Blazuj on the map?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Blazuj is number 2. That was the barracks in Blazuj, actually. And for as long as I've been alive, the barracks have been there, with the JNA soldiers there. Now, after 1991, in the autumn, the reservists came in there from Montenegro and Serbia. I would see them personally. In our fields and meadows, above my village, they were drawing maps, and on one occasion we actually --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was an occasion you've spoken about in your -- in a couple of your statements; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement from 1993, you mention being taken to Zunovnica, to load ammunition from the weapons store there. Have you been able to mark the location of Zunovnica on that map?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were you loading?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Grenades, infantry weapons, mines, that kind of thing, small arms, infantry arms. And we loaded that up from the last warehouses, because our people, the Bosniaks, stormed the area from Brezovaca and took this away. So they were withdrawing that equipment from the central point in the barracks, where they had concrete hangars. So we took -- drove the trucks in there and loaded and unloaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were under guard while you were offloading that ammunition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how were the guards dressed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Their police wore camouflage uniforms, olive-green ones. The rest of them had the JNA-type uniform, army equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Now, leaving that map aside for a time, and going back both in time chronologically to the beginning of your statements and period before the outbreak of war. You mentioned the visit of one neighbour, Goran Todorovic, to your settlement to ask for a surrender. Now, what ethnicity was Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's not Goran, but Gavro, Gavro Todorovic, and he was a Serb. Up until the war, we were great friends, so that I trusted him. I had more trust and confidence in him than some of my family members. But due to force of circumstance, he seemed to change and then he didn't want to see me any more, not only me, but my relatives, my brothers, and all the other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music just tell me: How was Mr. Todorovic dressed at the time he visited you? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He was wearing the olive-green JNA-type uniform. But also stationed there was a telephone from -- brought in from Blazuj to his house, in the autumn. And he didn't deny that. He told us that that was the case. And he also told us not to go out once.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could just interrupt you, Mr. Music. This is information that you've given to us in your statement from 1997; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these are statements which are now evidence, exhibits before the Trial Chamber, and they're aware of the content of these statements and they'll be able to read them and study them, and these questions are just by way of clarification to what you've said previously.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to move further now. You mention Djukanovic came to ask for surrender; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How was he dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He wore the same thing, the olive-green uniform, and he had a white band on his arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also talk about one Dragan Pusara calling for surrender through a megaphone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know it was Pusara who was calling for surrender?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him. It was about a hundred metres away as the crow flies. And as we knew that he was a Vojvoda and led all those men, all the ones that took part in the attack on the village and the torching of the village and so on, that's how. And I also had some binoculars and was able to look through them. I was a hunter for 50 years, so I was able to monitor his movements with those binoculars and his arming and so on. And we were powerless to do anything to stop him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the -- Djukanovic and Pusara are both ethnic Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Two men named Elcic who came into your home to detain you, what's their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were also Serbs. And their mother came from the village, so I knew them, although Tomo worked in the Coca-Cola factory with me for many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talk about, in paragraph 3 of your 1993 and 1998 statement, and paragraph 28 of your ICTY statement, you talk about your capture, and you describe your capture by a large group of people. You put the number of captors at between 50 and 60. Now, if we could just talk about that group of people for a minute. Could you tell us whether they were in uniform or in civilian clothes, and if they were in uniform, what kind of uniform were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Their police wore camouflage uniform, the olive-green type, whereas all the support and the rest of the police force wore the JNA uniforms and they had helmets too, whereas the other policemen did not have helmets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Among those captors, you mention an individual by the name of Rade Veselinovic. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb by ethnicity, and he was a hauler, a transporter, up until the war. And he provoked me most during the time I spent at Hadzici, and he provoked my wife as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mention seeing the bodies of three men by the house of Alija Music. Were these three men any close family relation to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Alija Music and Dervis Music were uncles. They were my father's brothers. And Fadil, he was my father's cousin. So they were all related in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to provide you and the Trial Chamber with a photograph bearing the number 00520200-35. If it could receive an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will have the reference P409, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you saw that photograph yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see in the picture before you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That is the Municipal Assembly now. We were detained in the first garage here, the one that's black. That's where I stayed. 47 men were there while I was there. That's where we were examined. You see where the green car is, that window.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, I was just trying to ask you -- you're pointing with your pen, and the Trial Chamber is not in a position to see what you're pointing to. I wonder if you can describe what you're pointing to. I wonder if we could -- are we in a position to put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we put it on the ELMO, we can follow the witness when he points at something, and if you would then describe that, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, with the pointer, could you show the Trial Chamber where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Music, you're invited to point at it on the ELMO so that we can see it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating the garage door to the far right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mr. Music, at the point where I interrupted you, you mentioned something about a green car. What were you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were questioning me here, where this window is. That's where we were beaten and things like that. And now you see this window here? That's where the toilet was. When people would enter the door -- through the door here, then that's where they'd beat us. Anyway, they wanted to. They beat Mujcic [phoen] the most. I think they questioned him about ten times. When we went to Lukavica, and that's what he told me, since he had a business of his own, they kept asking for money and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, does this photo of this building you call the Municipal Assembly building look like the building as it did in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. No. It didn't burn then. When the Dayton Agreement was signed, as they were leaving, they torched it. See? It was burned here, and it looked like this before. But it didn't look like this then. They had a normal roof and windows and doors and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When the witness was pointing, Ms. Edgerton, the place where he was beaten, he was pointing at the two openings in the wall directly behind the white and the green car.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, leaving that photo aside and moving on to another photo, which I'd ask be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before we move on from that photo, Your Honour, perhaps an indication from the Prosecution as to when the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is a date on it, Ms. Loukas, but unless there's any reason to believe it was not taken on the 16th of June, 1997 then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because often with these things the correct date is not on the photograph. You cannot necessarily trust the computer generated aspect on the bottom of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there -- Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was taken on the 16th of June, 1997, and you see me at the bottom right-hand corner of the picture wearing a long red skirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hadn't noticed that yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nor had I, Your Honour. I don't think we've got Ms. Edgerton on the -- well, I can't recognise her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different matter. But this is -- although it's not evidence, it's firsthand information. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could -- we'll remove that photo and put another photo on the ELMO after it receives an exhibit number. The next one bears the ERN number 00500200-20, also taken on the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr. Registrar, that this will be P410.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, now looking tell next photograph on the ELMO, you had an opportunity to view that photograph yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The sports hall where I was detained, together with my neighbours, friends, relatives, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at the moment you have your pointer on the -- what looks like an entry way to the bottom right-hand side. Could you point to the location or the entry way to the area where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The entry way was here, so that no one could run away. As for the inside, it's all in there, yes. But I never told you this: In September, towards the end of September, they threw shells here, see? You can see the holes here. We were hit by shells, and 20 people were wounded. I avoided all contacts, because I was the only survivor among all the families that were brought to these camps. But see the shell marks here? I never told you about that. I noticed it just now. So all the glass was shattered then, and then we had to clean it. We were lying on the concrete floors. It was very cold. It rained. As for the interior, you know what it's like. It's a sports hall, basketball can be played there. I cannot give you the exact number of metres, how big a basketball hall should be, but I'm sure that 1.000 people went through there. Because it changed. Some Serbs were taken away, who had money and friends and who paid for getting out. I have a neighbour, you see --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there. I note that for the record the witness is pointing to what appears to be damage to the roof of the building on the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whereas he was pointing to the right portion, just right from the middle of the photograph and he pointed at the entry used, but also moved sometimes the pointer to the left part of what seems to be an entrance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, if we could leave that aside and move on further in clarifying your previous evidence or the evidence in your statements, I'd like to talk about your transfer into the Sarajevo area. You mentioned you drove by -- you were driven by bus. Could you tell me if the drivers of the bus, buses, were in uniform or not, as far as you could see.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in olive-green/grey uniforms of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, once you had arrived at the gate to Kula prison, you talk about people boarding the bus and beating the prisoners. Were these people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had camouflage uniforms. When we came to the Kula gate, that's where we were supposed to be put up. I have no idea why they didn't let us -- I don't know whether the warden was there or not. Some people went missing too. But they beat us, and then they threw ammunition and they said: Look, balijas have ammunition. My father-in-law sat on the first seat and I was in the back. My father-in-law was born in 1926, so he participated in the other big war before that. And you can imagine what it was like. They beat us. They stubbed out cigarettes on our necks and things like that. You can imagine what it was like. Then there were some people on the Bosnian side, Dobrinja. We stayed there for an hour or two or whatever. It seemed like eternity to me. I was praying to God that they kill us and that they get it over with. And then -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These are difficult times that you're recalling, I know, and I apologise, but I feel I ought to remind you again that this is something you've spoken about previously in your statements and these are now exhibits with the Trial Chamber, and they do have that evidence in front of them. What I'd like to ask you about next, if I could, is when you speak about arriving in the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks, you mention you were beaten by a gauntlet as you were leaving the bus, entering the barracks building, and including up the stairs. Do you recall whether this gauntlet of people were wearing uniform at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They all wore uniforms, but we didn't dare look. We were supposed to keep our hands on the backs of our heads and we were supposed to keep running. Then they entered the dormitories and they beat us when we went to the toilets. They used different objects to beat us. So I remember that a neighbour asked if he could go and use the toilet too, and I just heard the guard hit him on the back. And he fell. I heard the blow. I don't know his name or surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I ask you about the gauntlet --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt at this point, but I think it would be very useful, in view of the fact that we're going through this process on an 89(F) basis of attempting to elucidate or clarify four different statements. I think for future reference it might be useful to actually mention on the transcript which particular paragraphs we are currently elucidating or clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yell. I see Ms. Edgerton is nodding so she'll take your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course I can do that. That previously -- the point at which we're at now deals or arises from or relates to paragraph 6 of the statement from 1993 and paragraph 62 of the ICTY statement. And I'm dealing with the gauntlet that the witness had to run as he left the bus and went into the barracks building and up the stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, do you recall hearing anybody in this gauntlet speak as you were running past?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were swearing at us, cursing our balija mothers. This is what you get for Alija's state. There were all sorts of provocations like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember noticing anything in particular about their accent at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I stated that. When they called out my name, I recognised their accents as coming from Serbia and Montenegro, because for 18 months I did my service in Serbia, in Nis, to be precise. And then, while I stayed in Germany for five years, I had people from there working with me, and then also later on when I worked for Coca-Cola, I worked with people from Serbia and Montenegro. And then while I was still working for Coca-Cola, I travelled to Serbia and Montenegro and back. So I'm familiar with the accent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the witness is actually moved on to paragraph 7 of the 1993 statement, paragraphs 3 and 4 of the 1994, 70 to 73 of the ICTY statement, and 5 of the 1998 statement. He's talking about the calling out of the 48 prisoners in Lukavica barracks. Now, Mr. Music, in the paragraph numbers that I've just stated, you describe that gauntlet and say that the people in the gauntlet were wearing red berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to notice what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They all wore camouflage uniforms, red berets, judging by the way they spoke and by their accents, it's not that I'm 100 per cent sure; I'm 1.000 per cent sure that they were from Serbia. They were the members of the Special Forces from Nis, the Nis specialists. I mentioned that in my previous statement in December last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 7 of your 1993 statement, paragraph 4 of your 1994 statement, and 74 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about arriving in the next room and seeing three officers sitting at a desk. I'd like to know what led you to the conclusion that these were officers.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, they had ranks, they all wore uniforms. Since I recognised on my left-hand side, as I walked in, I was not supposed to put my head up, but there was a lot of blood all over. But on the left-hand side I did see my brother and I had to put my hands up and I was supposed to look only in front of me. The man from Serbia had a kind of Lika cap with a coat of arms, and I recognised him as being from Serbia. He said: Bre, where are you from? And then I said where I was from. And he swore at my mother. He cursed my mother, and then he said: Where are your sons? At the front line? And I said I have no sons. I have only daughters. And he said: What is this? We were supposed to see this man who had sons. And they confused me with my brother. Whereas my brother stayed at home with his retarded son. You can find that in my statement. It was this Montenegrin who was interrogating me, whereas the Serb who was with me, or rather with us, I don't know where he was from, but he did not mistreat me. And this man from Serbia hit me and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, that's right. We can find that in your previous statement. And just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- something further. I note at page 30, line 3 of the transcript, Mr. Music is referring to his statement in December of last year. That's when he testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it his testimony in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to paragraph 84, Mr. Music, of your statement to the Tribunal. And that's where you mention seeing or meeting a man who you identify as Slobodan Avlijas. Could you clarify for us where you saw Mr. Avlijas?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, I saw him while I was in Kula. He came to my room, since Semsic was a colleague of his, he graduated from law school together with him, so he came to visit him. And he then gave him a pack of cigarettes then, some kind of Serbian cigarettes, and he also gave him some Serb money, because that was the first time I saw it. And this money was changed at the time, so that was the first time I saw this money while I was in camp. And then he also took him out for coffee, so I saw him on that occasion. Later on I saw him yet again when I was on the commission for exchanges. Masovic [phoen] asked him about these people these 47 people who were missing. He said: Avlijas, where are these people? And then he said: Well, look, Amor, I tell you. But I was not there at all. I was in Bijeljina. And when I challenged that, when I said on which day he came there and what he did and all that, then he said: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, the question to you was: Could you clarify for us where you saw Mr. Avlijas. I fully understand that you would like to tell all of the story you know. We have access to that already in your written statements. If we would hear the stories of everyone who has experienced those times, it would take us another 10 to 20 years. I hope that you do understand. And that's the reason why this Tribunal has decided that it will allow the parties also to give written statements. And of course you're telling us a lot of details. Ms. Edgerton might be interested in very specific details. So if you would please very carefully listen to her questions and then specifically answer to the details she thinks are most relevant at this moment. I'm not saying that the others are irrelevant or that they are less important for you, but we are under some time restraint. So may I invite you to focus on exactly what Ms. Edgerton asks you. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you were able to recognise Mr. Avlijas because you knew him personally, you had known him from before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what his occupation was before the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He was a judge at the municipality in Hadzici. And he lived on the same floor where my father-in-law lives, in the building where the TO was, across the street from the municipality building that you showed me. It was less than a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, I'm again going to ask you. The question was what the occupation of Mr. Avlijas was. You answered that by saying that he was a judge at the municipality in Hadzici, and then you started telling us where he was living, et cetera, et cetera, where Ms. Edgerton only asked you at this moment what his profession was. So could I again ask you to focus specifically on those details asked by Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That having been answered, the last question having been answered in that way, he effectively anticipated my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a bit difficult, of course. You'll understand if we give guidance to the witness how to respond to your questions, that even it would be your next question he should first wait until that question is put to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. At this moment, Your Honour, what I would like to do is play two -- two telephone intercepts, both of which the witness listened to yesterday in their entirety, one of which was partially played previously before this court. I'm just looking at the time. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it approximately take you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we would have time to play the first one all the way through and then maybe break for the second one. And I should indicate, Your Honour, in line with the guidance you had previously given as regards these intercepts, I won't be asking the witness to offer contextual comments on these intercepts. It's merely the Prosecution's position that these intercepts relate to some of the incidents the witness has spoken about in his previous statements and detailed somewhat in his testimony. So we would have time if we began now to play one in its entirety. I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that you'll put some questions to the witness at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be wise to play one intercept first. Would you then immediately ask questions about it? Because otherwise it might not be fresh in his memory any more if we are half an hour later. So I leave it up to you. If you say I can deal with the first intercept, then ask a few questions, if that could be done, well, let's say within the next 12 minutes, then it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think playing the first one might push us over the time, Your Honour, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then perhaps play both of them after the break. We'll then now first have a break until 10 minutes to 11.00, if that would be convenient. Mr. Music, we'll have a break of some 25 minutes. We'll adjourn, unless you, Mr. Hannis, would -- you are standing. No, not to address the Court. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we'll do now is we'll proceed with the intercepts, one after the other, with a brief pause after the first. Now, the first intercept to be played was -- and Ms. Javier can correct me if I'm mistaken, but the first intercept to be played was previously played in part before this Trial Chamber and the CD received an exhibit number and that's P292. So in other words, the whole intercept has already been made an exhibit, but the Trial Chamber has only heard an extract from it, and we propose to play the intercept in its entirety, using the same number, obviously. And I would ask that the witness be given a B/C/S copy of the transcript, please, so he can follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's no objection to that procedure. We'll have to consider whether or not to give a new exhibit number to the transcript of this intercept or whether that appears sufficiently in the -- to say the 209 series.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The 292 series, that would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 292, yes. Sorry. We'll deal with that at a later moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, yesterday, with Mr. Hannis and myself, you listened to two intercepted conversations. I'm going to play those conversations for you again in sequence, one after the other. And I'd ask you to follow along on the transcript in front of you as best you can, please. The first conversation is dated 26 June 1992, between Momcilo Krajisnik and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we do not hear anything, neither do we receive any translation which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not getting any sound, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Ms. Edgerton, could we please restart, because the interpreters get no original B/C/S sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see from the booth the interpreters aren't receiving any sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No sound, Your Honour. Now we can hear the sound but it's not discernible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I -- in the beginning I hear the same as you do before you start translating, and I do understand that there's no start of any translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The technician is coming in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know what the problem is, which is mainly the first step to the solution?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no idea what the problem is, Your Honour, but while it would have been convenient, in fact, appropriate, to play the intercepts at this interval because they fit within the chronology of the evidence so far, we could move on and come back to them. It might be somewhat confusing for the witness, but we could do that for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Music, since we have some technical difficulties in playing the intercept, Ms. Edgerton moves now to another subject. But we'll come back to this later. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And failing the technician being able to achieve something, we'll try and work with the transcript, but I'd prefer just to proceed for now and see if they can fix this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. Music, I'd like to move forward in the chronology of what took place in 1992 to the point at which you were taken to the police station in Ilidza, and that principally begins at around paragraph 93 and onward from the ICTY statement. And I'd like to deal with the new information that you told us about over the course of the weekend. Now, Mr. Music, you've described in your statements that you were held with a small number of other detainees in a cell in the police station in Ilidza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, from this cell, I understand that you had some small --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this, I would be submitting it's not appropriate for any further leading in view of the nature of the material sought to be elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you do your utmost best, and otherwise, Ms. Loukas will remind you not to lead in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, could you tell us where this cell was located in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The cell in the police station at Ilidza was located in the middle of this building. As you go up to the chief on the floor above. So I could see everybody coming in and out, going up to the first floor. It was 25 times 20, a steel door. There was a toilet there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Music. What was 25 times 20, please?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The opening in the middle of the door, to allow air to come in. We had no windows, so this was a form of ventilation. And if they closed this partition, this small window, then we would be suffocating inside. The premises was used as a toilet previously, but as it was being used as a prison, there was sometimes two of us and as many as 12 of us at times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you could just clarify, then. There was a door to this cell with an opening. And where did that door look out onto?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You looked out onto the staircase and the entrance and exit to all the offices in the police station on the floor, on that storey. So I was able to see all the comings and goings, who was coming in and going out. On many occasions I saw many people I knew from Hadzici, but we weren't allowed to say anything to them because they kept the fact that this was in fact a camp confidential, a secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, again, the question was: Where did the door look out onto? You answered that question, and then you continued to give us information which -- well, may be relevant, but whether or not, if you would first wait for the next question by Ms. Edgerton and then we'll see what she'd like to know. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just in terms of the opening that you're describing in this door, you've mentioned 25 times 20 but I see you're holding your hands up. Are you demonstrating for the Trial Chamber the size of the opening in the door?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've said that this door looked out onto the staircase and the entrance and exit to all the offices in the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I've lost my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with that description of the cell and the viewpoint, could you tell us about the day in which you saw the accused at the police station in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you were inviting not to lead. I have never heard in my whole life a more leading question than this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, then would you permit the question whether or not he has ever seen the accused during the course of his detention in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially in view of the, I would say, of the view of the surprise, wouldn't it be proper to ask whether -- let me do it. Mr. Music, when you -- you said you had a view through that door. Did you see people -- because you said that you had a look at the -- let me just have a look. Did you ever recognise someone coming in or going one out one of the offices you could look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who did you recognise? First of all, perhaps: How many people did you recognise coming in and out? What number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: I knew many people. Many people from Hadzici, from the police, came there to see the chief, Tomo Kovac, who was there then. In mid-August, I saw Momcilo Krajisnik coming to the MUP at Ilidza, because Tomo Kovac was supposed to be replaced by Tihomir Glavas, who was in the police from the very beginning of the war in Hadzici. He was the chief of police. So that I did have an opportunity -- I did everything that was necessary. I threw out the rubbish, for example and things like that. But I was close to the door which was opened and the police were waiting there, the police station was there, and I was doing some cleaning, and they didn't know I was there. They didn't realise I was there. But they were talking to each other and they said: Momcilo Krajisnik came and Tomo Kovac was supposed to go and become minister of police. So I overheard that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you hear people talking about a visit of Mr. Krajisnik or did you see Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw a car arriving, but I stood apart because I saw an escort, I knew that somebody was coming. So I stood by the window, by the police, where the door was always open if I -- if they needed me to do anything, to clean an office or anything like that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. The question was whether you heard people saying that Mr. Krajisnik visited the police station or did you actually see Mr. Krajisnik yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of their conversation, I heard them say that he had come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was whether it was just that you heard them saying that he visited or did you see him yourself? Perhaps we limit ourselves to the last question. Did you with your own eyes see Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. Straight afterwards, they brought me in and I was coming in through the opposite door, not the main entrance not the main door. Because we were on the opposite side and I recognised the man. I recognised him when he was coming back, when he was returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you in your cell or were you not in your cell when you say you saw Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the cell. I was in the cell. They had taken me back to the cell to prevent me from seeing too much. But I just happened to see it because the door was slightly ajar. I was standing by the door. And I saw that happen. And they were saying that he was supposed to come. I didn't know what the gentleman was doing there, because I was in the camp, so I didn't know the general situation and the goings-on, what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you saw him through the window in the door or through an opening, the door not being fully closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the opening. The door was closed, but through the opening. They would always lock the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was ajar. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The small window on the door was slightly ajar, was slightly open, and we would have suffocated had they not let that small window on the door open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that there was a kind of a closing to that small window so you could close it or you could open it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said it was -- do I understand you properly that you said it was almost closed but not entirely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not entirely, no. They would leave it open for some air to come in, to prevent us from suffocating. As it was a WC, there was water there all the time and I was wet myself all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how many people were in your cell at the moment when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was alone on that occasion, because my colleague, the driver, had taken away the dredger. They took away from the Muslims and Croats everything that was valuable. So we were driving this to the warehouse up there in Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you told us that you saw Mr. Krajisnik. How long would you be able to see him? Did he pass by? Did he stand still? Did he ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just while he was moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was he moving in what direction? From left to right or away from you, from the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he knew that I was there then, because when he -- he was coming in, I said that the car arrived in the compound --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, I was not asking whether Mr. Krajisnik was aware, but I was asking in what direction he moved when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the exit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Towards the exit. Did he come from the right or did he come from the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sitting like this, as I am now, and he passed in front of me, just a metre away. He was just going -- moving towards the next door, up the stairs, two metres from the stairs to the cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what height approximately was the opening in the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the opening was at the level of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be approximately in the middle of the door, taking into account the average height of a door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Higher. More, higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be higher. Could you give us an indication then how high.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me explain it to you like this: On one occasion, one of them knelt down, crouched down. The other man got up on his shoulders and they urinated on us and then they threw in acid at us. So the only way he could do this was to stand on his colleague's shoulder and then they closed the door on us. And a Serb, he was decent person and opened the aperture because we start coughing and our eyes starting watering. So if I were to stand up, it would be on a par at the level of my chin. And I was able to see them go for lunch or I could see everybody coming in and out. And I could recognise them by their voices. I knew who was going by. Even if the door was closed, you know, when you're in the camp for such a long time, you could recognise people's footsteps. And I asked them to let me move around and do the most menial of jobs just to get me out of that cell and to survive and get through that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've not yet answered my question whether he came from the left or from the right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was coming back. He was going back. I was here and he was going back. So he was passing by the staircase. I could see his head and I can see everything. I don't know why he was coming. I learnt that when I heard them talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you've now told -- given me a lot of information, but still not answered my question. Did he come from the left when he went to the exit or did he come from the right when he went to the exit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, coming from the left. He was passing by the staircase right by me, just like this screen in front of me. All I was aware of then was that I had seen him. I never thought I'd survive and have to explain it all to you here before you. Had I known that I was coming here, well, then I might have paid more attention so that I could describe it more exactly to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on to the next point, and I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was by my questions was exhausted. I have to be quite clear to you: I have not seen the additional information. I've not read it. I've not even seen it at this moment. I know that it does exist. So my questions were entirely on the basis of, I would say, of a blank mind. So I would not mind if you have any further questions, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To my mind, this issue, what's come out into evidence as regards this issue has been satisfactorily covered and I'd like to move on to the next point now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, dealing with paragraph 10 of your 1993 statement and paragraph 103 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about your return to the sports centre in Hadzici, where you found there were approximately 500 detainees. Could you tell us: Did you have any immediate family members present in that group of 500?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My late father was there. He died immediately after leaving the camp. Then there was my brother, my sister-in-law, my brother's son, who's retarded, his other son, who was born in 1981, my wife, Zumreta Music, then a cousin of mine, Hamid Music, and his wife Hasnija Music.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from conversations with the other detainees, did you learn where they were from, where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were all locals from Hadzici. They all -- Gadici [phoen], Dupovici [phoen], those hamlets, Donji Hadzici, from all the different hamlets, and I knew practically every single person who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now dealing with paragraph 11 of your 1993 statement and paragraphs 108 to 112 of your ICTY statement. You talk about your transfer to Svrake and the situation there. And at this point, I'd like to show you a photo, a further photo, which -- bearing the number 03616938, which has an exhibit number from this Trial Chamber, number P379. It was previously shown. I have both copies of the photo here, but Mr. Registrar might ... If a copy could be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness would like to point something out on the ELMO. Maybe we could have the usher just shift the picture up a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please have the ELMO moved such direction that the whole of the picture appears. A little bit higher up even.
