utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Up a little more, please. I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, did you have occasion to have a look at this photograph yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: This is in Svrake, Planja's house, called Duja [phoen] camp. We would go up here. That was the entrance, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating the entrance on the left-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The entrance was here, and I was up here, on this upper storey, here, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And does this --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That was where the police were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating the second -- one of the second-floor windows; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, does this depict the picture of what you call Planjo's house resemble how it appeared in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 11 of your 1993 statement, you say you found 102 detainees there on your arrival. From conversations with those other detainees, did you learn where they were from? You can remove the photo now.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: From talking to the people, I learnt that they were from the Semizovac, Svrake, Ahatovici area, Bioca, and I think it belongs to the other municipality, Visoko, Visoko municipality. Because I have some family there and I came across some cousins and relations on my father's side who took me in. So I went upstairs, where they were lying down. They spent the whole night on the staircase. They were good people. And they went to be a human shield at Zuc later on and to dig trenches and things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, now if we could just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to put another document, a document to the witness at this point, and I think Ms. Javier has gone to the AV booth. And maybe the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher. Could you assist Ms. Javier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a series of documents. Actually, a collection of two groups, bearing the ERN number 00577933 to 00577938, with one single page at the end with a different ERN number, 02100578. All dated 22 October 1992. If that could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will receive the number P412 -- 11, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, in your -- in paragraph 11 of your statement from 1993, you noted that you were transferred to Svrake on 23 October 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Music, did you have an opportunity to look at these two documents yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you can read Cyrillic, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: A bit. I prefer the Roman alphabet, but I can read Cyrillic too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you able to -- you reviewed these documents. Were you able to understand what was contained in them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Turning to -- having looked at these documents, then, Mr. Music, could you, for the Court, tell us what these documents are.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The document speaks for it was, and the witness not having been someone who has, prior to being interviewed by the Prosecution citing these documents, it seems to me there's very little -- no probative value in relation to that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It depends what the following questions will be. I take it, Ms. Edgerton, an explanation in presence of the witness might not be the most appropriate thing to do. Let me first ask: Mr. Music, do you read or understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I take it that you really do not understand -- you cannot follow a conversation, you cannot read a line in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist and ask the witness to take off his headphones. Ms. Edgerton, what in the next questions would be such that the witness could cast a specific light on these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the question clumsily. I can offer the same details that I was hoping to elicit from the witness. This purports to be a document dated 22 October 1992, or several documents under that date, the first being a letter from minister Momcilo Mandic to the president of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, the president of the RS, the chairman of the Assembly and the prime minister, the second being a report on the situation in prisons and collection camps for prisoners of war, also with the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But what could this witness add to that? I mean apart from -- if his testimony is that -- well, let's say he was detained in place X or Y and if that same place appears in this letter, then even without asking the witness, the Chamber is still able to see that his testimony seems to correspond with what's in this letter. But what could the witness add, apart from that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Simply that, Your Honour, in fact he will confirm that he was one of the prisoners of war accommodated in the Hadzici sports centre, as set out in paragraph 10, I think it is, of the first report. And with regard to the last document, letter to the Serbian municipalities of Hadzici and Ilidza, signed by minister Momcilo Mandic, directing that these detainees be transferred to Svrake, he can confirm that his transfer to Svrake took place immediately after the date of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, I can indicate that the bundle of documents we received, and I'm just confirming with Ms. Cmeric, has two documents with translations, not the third document that Ms. Edgerton is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. What I -- yes. But the third document might be the one that was just given to us and not yet attribute a number. Is that correct? Then it should have been given to the Defence as well. Is that the document, the 22nd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see that it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you receive that, Ms. Loukas? It was just handed out to us now, a document with a number -- well, English translation, last four digits is 0578, which is an ET number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think we're getting it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Take your time to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, in view of the response given by Ms. Edgerton, is there any further submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one correction in relation to the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That very last document in the B/C/S refers to prelog attachment, but the translation is argument number 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prelog means attachment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prelog means attachment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But the English translation is argument. So there's been a mistranslation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I see that it says number 4, 48, whereas I can see if broj stands for number, then I see 48 but not 4, 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. So that's the issue. It's just a mistranslation in terms of attachment to argument in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, Ms. Edgerton, it bears the page 623 and it seems to be an attachment number 48. To what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks to me like -- I have an English translation of the same document without these handwritten annotations at the top, bearing a different ERN number. So I don't know that I'm able to assist except to say that it appears we have two separate copies in our systems of the same document, one with handwritten annotations and the other without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then preferably the English translation should correspond with the version that is provided in original. So you're working from a different document. Ms. Loukas, could we proceed on the basis that the Chamber expects, in view of the answer just given by Ms. Edgerton that she might come up with a document where we start with Republika Srpska and whereas 623 and the prelog number doesn't appear and where we have a different ERN number. She has an original. Ms. Edgerton, could you give me the original for one second that you're working from? Because then I can compare whether it looks more or less the same and then ... Yes, Mr. Usher. Could you please assist Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that we all might have the same original, but I might have a translation of a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see you have -- yes. Your translation was a different ERN number, and your translation does not correspond with the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We should rectify that as soon as possible. And it appears there's two copies of the same document, possibly retrieved from different individuals or different locations. And I'll make sure the matter is rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please return this to Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now that that translation error has been clarified and we look forward to the clarification in relation to the documents, the question Your Honour asked me in relation to whether there was any response in light of Ms. Edgerton's response on this question of the documents that are sought to be put to the witness. Your Honour, I would submit that the position put by the Prosecution does not in any way detract from the argument that I have made, and that is, firstly, the documents speak for themselves. If there is any inferences to be drawn, they are, of course, to be drawn by Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in the usual course. In the circumstances, it appears quite clear that the witness can in no way add anything to the question of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't think, and I'm now referring to the information Ms. Edgerton gave us. I don't think that this witness could tell us anything about the reporting as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, and we do not need, as a matter of fact, this witness to tell us that if he reads in a report that there was a detention facility in Hadzici and if he has testified that -- and even that it's in the sports centre, where we have seen a photograph of that sports centre, and where this reports says that, that if the witness would conclude that it most likely would be the same, then we even do not need the witness to come to a -- at least it would allow us to come to a similar conclusion, not saying that we do, but ... So to that extent ... On the other hand, Ms. Loukas, then we still have the problem on how this document could be introduced. Would the Defence in any way object to the admission of this document if it would be more or less clear where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my objection is based on the fact that it is inappropriate for this particular document to be dealt with through this witness. It's also clear, Your Honour, that we're dealing with a document that does have a signature, does apparently have a stamp in the B/C/S version, but is obviously a document to be dealt with through another witness at another time, considering the person who has signed it and the witnesses to come, Your Honour. And in those circumstances, it's certainly not a document to be dealt with through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you say that we could draw our own conclusions, then of course we would need the document to be in evidence. Therefore, I'm just inquiring whether there would be a chance to have this document -- I'm not saying that it would be the proper way to introduce it through this witness. Then the second document is a bit different. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber comes to the conclusion that the witness can testify of what he experienced, and that is his detention and his detention in Hadzici and when he was transferred. That's all fine. But he really could not add anything to these documents. So, therefore, it's not a proper way to introduce these documents, through this witness. I leave it open whether they could be introduced without a witness at all or just supported by some information, where they come from, perhaps after you've given this information to the Defence and see whether it would still be necessary to call any witness to testify about the source of these documents. But this witness would not be a proper one to introduce these documents into evidence. So I'm not saying anything about the relevance. The Chamber is not saying anything about whether they could be introduced or not. But at this moment, you were asking the witness for the obvious, I would say. If you know his testimony, if you know the document, this witness is not in a special position, I would say, to draw these inferences. So therefore, this is not a rejection of the document, but at least a non-admission at this moment through this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I also think that we should reverse the attribution of the number to this document, Mr. Registrar, so that P411 would be for the next document rather than for this one. Ms. Edgerton, the other document, the photograph, was already in evidence, so we don't have to deal with that number. It doesn't need any change.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- just before Ms. Edgerton proceed, just for the record, I can indicate that -- and we obviously don't need to deal with it at this point, but I do want to place it on the record. There are significant translations errors with the documents we're dealing with that we've been dealing with right now. I want to place that on the record before we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we do is invite Ms. Edgerton to review the translation if she wants to come back with this document. The invitation is there, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps during the next break, Ms. Loukas, you could assist Ms. Edgerton in pointing at what the problems are.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That would bring us to the last -- if the witness could put his earphones back on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your patience, Mr. Music. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that brings us to the last two items, the intercepts, and I'm told by Mr. Hannis that before playing them we need a five-minute break in which the technicians have to come in and do something technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. So therefore you suggest that we have a break now. Yes. Let's then have a five minutes' break, and if everyone could remain standby. We'll have a break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, have all the technical problems been solved?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I've been told. And there's been a rehearsal and we're prepared to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I do not hear. So if you put on your microphone, then the first technical problem is solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first -- and as I said without the microphone, there's been -- Ms. Javier has done a rehearsal and it looks like we'll be ready to play the intercepts now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that we follow the same procedure as we did before, that if it goes too far, the interpreters are interpreting on the basis of the written text, and at the same time, the other interpreter, by following, will see whether there are any inconsistencies, the procedure that has been elaborated before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first intercept now being one, Mr. Music, dated 26 June 1992, between Momcilo Krajisnik and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've listened to this yesterday, and have the same transcript that you reviewed yesterday in front of you again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We can begin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Miljana: Hello. Minister, how are you. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. How are you. Miljana: Just a moment, please. The president would like to talk to you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Mandic? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Are you a traitor like everybody else. Momcilo MANDIC: God forbid. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes? Miljana: Minister, the connection broke up. Momcilo MANDIC: Something at your end ... Miljana: You can, laughing. Momcilo MANDIC: From the village up there, and then you got cut off. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, president? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What was it? Momcilo MANDIC: Probably something at your end. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: The moment I told you and you betrayed it, the line got cut off. Momcilo MANDIC: God forbid. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Ah. Momcilo MANDIC: I would not do it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo, tell me, how does it go? Momcilo MANDIC: Well, I'm not up to date with what is going on in that lower part, the main one, but as for this one, it is going well. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: ... these haven't come in at all. Momcilo MANDIC: Not at all? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Not at all. Momcilo MANDIC: I would not know anything about that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: This is a shame, a shame. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Two things. I actually wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see with him what is happening with this, so it means that what we agreed upon was not respected. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There is still a half chance today, and tomorrow it will be finished. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It's a big problem with Alija. Has that one been finished. That is awful. As of today we finish it all, you know. Momcilo MANDIC: Here, there is something pounding. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Momcilo MANDIC: It could be heard that they pound. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. That is -- has he made it down there or not? It's all over now. Secondly, have you released the one I told you about by any chance? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, I have. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes? Momcilo MANDIC: He left for Vrbanja one hour ago. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Thank God. Momcilo MANDIC: Karamehmedovic, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, that's him. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, he is gone. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let me also ask you about what this Savic Milos, since it's his brother that is really -- Momcilo MANDIC: President, I put it on the list. The first next exchange and it will be finished. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Check it down there. Do you have anyone there? Can you contact someone? Momcilo MANDIC: There is this Vukovic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb who is criticising us because we have four hundred prisoners here, you know? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who is criticising? Momcilo MANDIC: I've got four hundred. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And who is criticising? Momcilo MANDIC: This Vukovic, Filip, the member of the youth organisation, Serb, he says clean it but for them they are ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Filip Vukovic? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Communist? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What does he want? Momcilo MANDIC: He is the president of that exchange commission. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Their commission? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And what is it that he wants? Momcilo MANDIC: War prisoners. No, they are ex for them. They are hardly interested in people. They are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanja, go to their own people. He says that's ethnic cleansing, what we do ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He does. Momcilo MANDIC: Here ... When ... I will fucking -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And where is he now? Momcilo MANDIC: Somewhere there. I do not know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: With them, isn't he? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That means he is theirs? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: God, traitors all around. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good, Momo. Look, please do call him. I would like to help Savic. It's his brother in stake. Momcilo MANDIC: First exchange, I will take care of that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good, Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: And that man, is he gone? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo, let me ask you something. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Whom would we appoint for the republic [sic] prosecutor. Momcilo MANDIC: Avlijas Slobodan. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Avlijas Slobodan? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well is that -- Momcilo MANDIC: It is, president. Here, there is a man who knows everything who is from here. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know him. Momcilo MANDIC: So, you do know him? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. If he was pro ... Judge ... Momcilo MANDIC: He was medj ... He was in my ministry, however, he is skilled, capable, he knows many of those people, and the place does not hold him. I think he is the man for it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Kovac Slobodan. This one cannot. Momcilo MANDIC: Kovac Slobodan? What. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. Momcilo MANDIC: Already. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You should draft that proposal and then send it from here. Momcilo MANDIC: Deal. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Momcilo MANDIC: Bye. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Come on, go back to work. You are hardly there yourself ... Really... Listen, you say I will give the fax and you do it straight away and you say I will give the phone and you do it straight away. Momcilo MANDIC: Laughing. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We should set you free from this fax because ... Momcilo MANDIC: Don't ... Will come ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You don't have to ... Momcilo MANDIC: Skrbo is here. I don't know what to do with him. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Don't go to the field now, for action ... Momcilo MANDIC: Laughing ... no, no, no ... President, what are we going to do? Send a commissioner to Kasindol, two -- three men, some Papazi they came to me from Dr. Avramovic from Kasindol. Nobody ever called. They scattered there, doctor. They appoint their own people for directors. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And who is that one? Momcilo MANDIC: To Kasindol, the hospital. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who are these people? Where is that from? Momcilo MANDIC: Local community of Kasindol, the Crisis Staff. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Is that the municipality, which one? Momcilo MANDIC: No, it's the local community Ilidza. Ilidza is the municipality. Kasindol is local community. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And why do they have the commissioner? Why don't they go there? Momcilo MANDIC: No, it isn't. I don't know which ... These doctors came to me. They appointed some ... Divljan Sonja instead of this director ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And how could they do that? Momcilo MANDIC: The Crisis Staff of the local community Kasindol appointed her. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Give me, please ... Momcilo MANDIC: And then ... Popovic Koviljka, the cashier, to make an overview to see how the income is being distributed, and income again ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will call Prstojevic to go there or to send someone because he has the Crisis Staff Ilidza, that is Ilidza. Momcilo MANDIC: It's a shame president. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will see that they are taken care of immediately [as interpreted]. Momcilo MANDIC: But they are in contact with Prstojevic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: See, then if he does not do anything we'll see to send someone else there. Momcilo MANDIC: They are in some kind of business with that Prstojevic Jevic. They do black marketing together ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He cannot do anything on his own, he has the committee now, some wonderful people are there, you know. They are not the old ones any more. Momcilo MANDIC: But, doctor, these came, and they whine and cry ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Tell them it will be taken care of properly. Momcilo MANDIC: Because they do not obey. They did not give them a slice of bread. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who? Momcilo MANDIC: Those from the local community because ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who does not give a piece of bread? Momcilo MANDIC: They would not allow assistance go straight to the hospital Kasindol but only through them. Then they stop that assistance and give them a little. It's a shame. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will now ... Momcilo MANDIC: People should be arrested, President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will find Dragan Kalinic to go there and see what needs to be done. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, please, doctor, do that. Here I have five people sitting right across me staring at me and ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo, what you promised I will do. Momcilo MANDIC: Good, President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There is no such minister in the entire planet ... Momcilo MANDIC: Oh, come on, please ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will ... Momcilo MANDIC: So they don't disperse the staff. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will, Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: Thank you very much, bye."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you've listened to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've understood everything you've heard?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, before -- after listening to this conversation or while listening to this conversation and before looking at the transcript, were you able to recognise any of the speakers, the voices of any of the speakers in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How were you able to recognise those voices?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I knew them before the war, before the operations started. As for Momcilo Mandic, I saw him at the Kula several times. He came there where we were given food. My window faced --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, if I can just make you step back for a couple of seconds. When you say I knew them before the war, do you mean you had personal acquaintance with them before the war or you had had occasion to hear their voices some other way?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. Hearing their voices over TV, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said that one of the speakers in this conversation was Momcilo Mandic. Did you ever have occasion to see a person who was identified to you as Mandic visit Kula during your detention there?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it's entirely clear to me. Again, Ms. Edgerton, you're doing exactly the same, although you use a few more words, but you're doing exactly the same. You're leading the witness in one of the really sensitive issues. And that's done. Not to make the questioning of the Chamber the example for your future conduct, but perhaps you could try to remind how I put a few questions to this witness in relation to visitors in detention facilities and try to do it as neutrally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He did offer that evidence up before I had interrupted him, in fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that. And that would not be a sufficient justification just to take that then for granted and to feel freely to lead as you did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, other than --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Other than seeing either of these individuals on TV, did you have occasion to personally see them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. But I know that Momcilo Krajisnik is from Zabrdje, and I have a friend from [indiscernible], that's right above his village, and I know his wife is also a teacher and I know where his house is and everything. I watch television, because they figured prominently even before the war and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. So that's about Mr. Krajisnik as a speaker. Now, you mentioned that you recognised the voice of Mr. Mandic as a speaker. Other than seeing Mr. Mandic on TV, did you have occasion to see him face to face?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of seeing him face to face because he came to Kula, right opposite my window that was facing the canteen. He and his brother. He has a receding hairline and has light-coloured hair and was on the police force before the war. I know everything. So I had the opportunity of seeing him then, but not after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Music, you said that you saw him in Kula. Could you tell us how often you saw him during the course of your detention there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact number because there was a dog tied beneath our window and we did not dare come to the window, and therefore we were not allowed to see them. The guards even threatened that they would beat us if we would come close to the window, because they didn't want us to see who was coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Several occasions. They either came for coffee or for lunch or for breakfast, whatever. Many of them came. But I was interested in that least of all. I was hoping to have food or something like that. I worked on the 20th of July, 1992, in Ozrenska Street. We were digging trenches and dugouts and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you've spoken about your work on Ozrenska Street in your statements which are before the Trial Chamber. I just have, before we get to the next intercept, one other question for you, and it deals with the number of detainees that you were aware of at Kula as of the date of this conversation. How many men were detained, to your knowledge, as of the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Since they separated 47 people out of the 280, I told you that, so you have the figures. But in the neighbouring buildings, I heard screams and cries, but I don't know how many people were in those buildings. Women, children were crying, people were screaming. They were beating us. They were forcing us to sing different songs, saying this is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. I think you've answered the question very well. And I think it's time for us to move on to the second conversation that you heard yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'd like to ask a few questions about the rather chaotic portions of the testimony until now. But Ms. Loukas, if there's anything you'd like to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just very quickly, Your Honour. I can understand what Ms. Edgerton is doing, but it's inappropriate for comments such as "you've answered the question very well." I can understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that I do understand that Ms. Edgerton wanted to express that the answer of the witness was sufficient as far as what she -- but let me just ask a few questions first before we move to our next subject. Mr. Music, you told us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that, if I understood you well, that you had seen Mr. Mandic several times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like you to concentrate on the first time you saw him. Where were you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only saw him in passing, only in passing, as he was entering the canteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first ask you: Where were you when you saw for the first time Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I was beaten quite badly in Kula and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was standing by the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were standing by the window --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in a cell or in a room or in a hall? Tell us what the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a room that had windows down the entire wall. There were 25 of us prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were in a room together with 25 prisoners and there was a large window going entirely to the floor or just a little bit up from the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were radiators, and then windows were above the radiators. So now you can visualise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say this window was -- you saw him going to the canteen. Was the canteen in the same building or in a different building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the building opposite. There's about 50 or perhaps 60 metres to it. It was shaped like a horseshoe, and there was a building going all around. That was where the camp is, where it was before the war and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you well that it was not in a different building, but it was in a different wing of the same building, opposite to the wing your room was in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now try to concentrate on the first time you saw Mr. Mandic going to the canteen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In camouflage, in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If you wait for the questions, then I'll ask you. I would like to know: Did he arrive walking to that building or by any means of transportation vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, no means of transportation vehicles came in, because they had a parking-lot elsewhere. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you want to explain your answer, but I'd rather first hear your answer before to receive the explanation. So you say he came walking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He came to the building and the building is longish, about 50 metres, and I saw them walking in. I saw him because I knew him before he was on the police force. I recognised him himself, and then he was saying that that was his brother. Because this man who was the colleague of Avlijas knew that. He knew them. Because he probably used to meet with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Mandic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not meet him. He was in the room and he was walking in the opposite direction. And I was as I am here, and they were 50 metres away from me when they were entering this canteen or mess hall or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have misunderstood your earlier testimony. Let's go back to it. You said: "I saw him because I knew him before. He was on the police force. I recognised him himself --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: : "He was saying that he was his brother." When was he saying to whom that he was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please explain, because then I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't saying it. It was this colleague who was visited by -- Judge Slobodan Avlijas said that was his brother. I didn't know the brother. I knew who Mandic was. I cannot say things that I did not know. But for me, it's a silly thing to say that you don't know someone who holds high office in any country. I mean, it's silly. You watch television. You know who is what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The only thing we'd like to know is what exactly you observed, by what means. So you say you knew who Mr. Mandic was because you had seen him on television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war I followed all of this, so I knew him from before. I did not know his brother, though. I know Krajisnik for many years. I did not know his brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus on the questions I'm putting to you. So you knew Mr. Mandic only by watching television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war, I knew him, because he was in the MUP. My cousin worked in the MUP, and different relatives of mine. I knew him. Just -- I knew that Tomo Kovac was in Ilidza in the police force there before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- try to make a clear distinction between what you have seen and what you know. You understand? I can say that I know who is the mayor of The Hague because I have seen this written down in newspapers. But at the same time, I might never have seen him live. Do you understand what I mean? So you knew what the position of Mr. Mandic was because other people told you and you watched that on television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I follow the newspapers and television, so I know all the faces of people who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who are in high positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So through the media and through what people told you, you were aware of the positions and of the faces of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever see Mr. Mandic live? Did you ever see him face to face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In passing, in the town of Sarajevo, before the war, for instance. But I wasn't interested in him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's go back to the first time you saw him when you were in Kula prison. He walked to the canteen; is that a correct understanding of what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a distance of approximately 50 to 60 metres; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you saw him at this distance, was it -- how did you recognise him? On the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know him. I'm following it all now, too. And I know the property and riches he possesses, I know about the people around him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me bring you back again. I'm not asking you what you know about Mr. Mandic and whether he's rich or poor. I'm asking you on the basis of what you recognised him at that first occasion when he went to the canteen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my colleagues said Mandic is coming in and his brother to have something to eat because the others went down there to clean up. I didn't because I was exhausted. So I didn't. I didn't move around. I had long hair and a beard and not even my friends could recognise me when they took me out to have my hair cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on the beginning of your answer. You said: "My colleagues said Mandic is coming in and his brother to have something to eat."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them going into the canteen. Whether they were eating, whether he they just went for a couple of coffee, I don't know. But I saw them coming in and when you're in the camp you just pray to God that you have enough food and freedom. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand that the position from which you observed what you just told us was not one that you would wish to be in. Now, did your colleagues recognise him and have they drawn your attention to his presence, or did you by yourself, before your colleagues said anything to you, already recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was standing there, and so were some other of my colleagues. They were standing next to me and we were looking in that direction. And I saw them coming in. I was not interested at all at who was what. But then had this man said there's Mandic and his brother and I had a better looked and recognised him because he had a receding hairline, didn't have much hair up in front and that's when I saw him. I saw him coming in. Otherwise, he didn't come to see me or mistreat me or anything like that or anybody else. So I can't say anything bad about him. I personally -- that's just what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your colleague drew your attention that the person that was going to the canteen was Mr. Mandic and his brother. Then you looked and you recognised him; is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any further information about his visit, reason of the visit, length of the visit, well, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let me take you back to an earlier part of your evidence. I have to find the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Mandic and the person who was told that was his brother, were you -- did you have a clear view over the terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, was the view in any way obstructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was walking around there. I said the dog was right underneath the window and the policeman was walking up and down and if he saw us at the door he would beat us and didn't want us to see who was coming in and going up because everybody, the higher officers, had their meals there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean that you were not close to the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was standing next to the window perhaps a metre away. I wasn't -- I didn't dare get right up against the window to avoid having the guard see me. But we looked out of the window all the time. We could not look out the window. If you were interested in something, you would look out. You weren't allowed to move around the room because there were 20 of us lying down on the floor. And I had been beaten a lot. So they said that I should stand up, that it would be better for my condition if I stood up for a while. I don't want to have to go into all these explanations now. But judging by the conversations I would be able to draw those conclusions. I'm not a judge to say who did what, when, how, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What conversations are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with respect to Mandic and all the rest of it. I wasn't able to ask him anything. I was smaller than a dog, as far as they were concerned, because they humiliated us, so they treated us worse than dogs. So I wasn't able to go up to him and ask him something. So you're asking me to tell you something that I just am not able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, as far as the other visits are concerned, was your observation of Mr. Mandic a similar one or same distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. It's like this, but we were all nervous wrecks because the abuse and mistreatment went on. They wouldn't let us go to the toilet even when we wanted to. So what -- we just had a litre and a half water among the 25 of us. It was general chaos, absolutely chaotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question -- my question, however, was whether you saw him in similar circumstances, that means same distance, same position, approximately, from where you observed him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we weren't allowed to stand right up to the window. We moved back a metre. So if the guard was walking up and down, he couldn't see us right up at the window. Otherwise, he'd take someone out and mistreat them, beat them. So we tried to steer clear of anything like that. And usually they were the people that came in from elsewhere who did that. Otherwise, the prison administration, they were very decent to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, again, I'm just trying to find out, when you told us that at -- when you if it first time saw Mr. Mandic, that you were at some distance, you said also approximately a metre away from the window, whether at the second time this was the same or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same. We weren't allowed to stand right up against the window. I've told you already. I don't want to repeat it ten times. I hope you've understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly have understood that. Do you remember how much time went by between the first and the second time you saw Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you, because I wasn't interested. All I was interested in was to have enough food to eat and for them to let me walk up and down. Who came in, what, how long, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many times all together you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate? Was it -- well, let's say -- I do understand more than once, but it could be five times, ten times, 20 times, 50 times. Could you give us a more precise answer than -- if you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I don't want to mislead you. I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even not approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to venture a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the purpose of the visit of Minister Mandic, apart from that you took it from him going to the canteen that he might go to eat there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this; you must understand: If you're a camp inmate, a prisoner, all you're thinking about is to have food and your own personal freedom, even if they beat you. I couldn't pick and choose. I didn't know why he was coming or going and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was he always accompanied by his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he accompanied by others when he was -- by another person or by other persons when he was not accompanied by his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they would come in, more of them. I didn't look to see who, what. They were all the same to me. They were all my enemies. So I didn't -- I never thought I would survive. And had I thought ever that I would survive, then I would pay attention to every detail, because my memory serves me very well. But if you can -- I'm just telling you in the briefest possible terms, because it's something that I feel strongly about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Music, please accept that no one is blaming you for not having seen or perhaps not remembering any details of what happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said you didn't know why he was coming, was that an answer to my question that you had no information about the purpose of his visit; you were not told why he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they take everything away from you, your ID, your papers, you haven't got a radio, you haven't got anything else, how could you know the purpose for them or him coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. [Indiscernible] your answer. Ms. Edgerton, you wanted to move to your next subject, but I think we're about to have a break, because it's 10 minutes to 1.00. After the break, I'd -- yes. I would first like to ask the usher to escort Mr. Music out of the courtroom. We have another break, Mr. Music, for approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, first of all, do you have any idea on how much time you'd still need for examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One or more intercept, two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more intercept, two questions. So approximately 15 minutes, if at least the Chamber doesn't interfere. Then one of the issues that will then arise is whether we could start with the cross-examination, and we understood, Ms. Loukas, that you are taken by surprise as far as the information of the presence of Mr. Krajisnik in the police station is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, the witness's evidence certainly contained even more surprises thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Ms. Edgerton, I take it that the -- well, the surprise parts that we have gone through them or are there still even more surprises to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there lies nothing more, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you're invited to explain to the Chamber, because that might be relevant for the question on whether there's any cross-examination needed or to what extent it is needed, Ms. Loukas, what the OTP considers that it has presented evidence to. Let me just give you an example. If you would say the testimony of this witness -- well, I'll invite you to tell the Court what, in your view -- to what extent, in your view, the -- especially the new elements of the evidence have contributed to the presentation of the Prosecution's case. You'll understand that there are quite a few options. If, for example, it would have been your purpose just to present evidence that Mr. Krajisnik has ever been in that police station, apart from what he did there, but just to prove his presence, that would perhaps be different from his presence with a specific purpose or ... We'd like to know that, because the Chamber wants to, to the extent possible, avoid unnecessary recalling of witnesses, and if a witness would have to be recalled for further cross-examination on an issue which at least is in the eyes of the OTP not the issue they think they have presented evidence on, then of course it would be not of great use. So you're invited to prepare for that. You'll get those questions after the break. By the way, do it right after the break or after we finish the examination-in-chief. We'll see that. Then we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, may I invite you to first answer the question put to you by this Chamber before the break, and that, of course, mainly is in relation to the testimony related to the presence of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Mandic at places where the witness was detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To speak first to the information about Krajisnik's presence at the police station in Ilidza, I just want to underline that we would, through this witness, not be seeking any further than that, the indication of his presence at the station at a date between 23 July and 8 September 1992. But over the break, I had some consultations with another member of my team whose knowledge extends to areas other than my own, which is basically limited to Sarajevo, and he said that the fact of his presence is something that, together with other evidence, might go to show knowledge on the part of the accused of a detention facility in -- or in Ilidza at the police station or other detention facilities in the area. But more importantly, in a way, it would eventually be part of an argument or be used with other evidence as part of an argument to show the accused's influence over high-level police officials. My colleague advised me that the date, the time frame of the alleged visit of Mr. Krajisnik to this police station would correspond temporally with the shift of police power from Ilidza up to the north-east part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Bijeljina. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- we have limited information about reason of, well, what is said to be the visit of Mr. Krajisnik, apart from other matters as far as the reliability of the observations. Wasn't the reason that this particular police chief, but perhaps you could tell us what was, according to his evidence, exactly the reason of the visit, as he was told by others, which of course is hearsay, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand, and I don't have the transcript to scroll up in front of me, but I understand his testimony to be that Mr. Krajisnik's presence there had to do with the removal of Tomo Kovac, who was at the time the police head there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Removal, promotion, transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, promotion and removal is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. Promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Promotion, of course, is -- do you know what, in your evaluation, promotion to what? Wasn't it in ministerial post somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I believe the witness described it as a ministerial position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's your perception that then the relevance of such a visit would not be primarily that you'd say: I'd like to see who potentially would become a minister, and if it is a person that is a police officer at that time, then the emphasis is rather on the control of the police forces than on being interested to know who is going to be a minister?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We would be relying on -- your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a little bit of both, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just put it very sharp. If the person would have to become a minister would have been a -- well, let's say a director of a beer brewery, if you go and see such a person, would that primarily indicate your interest in beer factories or would it rather be interested in persons who become a minister? I know that the comparison, of course, is, as all comparisons, not a perfect one, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it would represent an interest in the person who is to become a minister. And not being aware of other evidence which might be coming before this Trial Chamber, there may well be other evidence presented and I understand it is the plan to show that, apart from mere interest, that the accused was in effect in a position to assure the promotion and its being effected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not an inference that you could make on the basis of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So therefore ... Yes. About the existence of detention facilities, wasn't the evidence of the witness that the visitor might not have even noticed him being there in detention?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He -- yes. He did mention, though, that he was within close proximity of another facility, the graphic arts facility, which in documentation that was under discussion and Your Honour issued a ruling on, is listed as one of the other detention facilities in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that if you visit a police station in the same area, you should be aware of the existence of a --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's in immediate proximity, in fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we have not heard any evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I was about to say, the witness said because he was in fact so well hidden you might not have known of his existence there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that also means that from this evidence at least, it's difficult to draw the inference that someone who visited that police station under those circumstances might be aware of any detention at all, apart from that you might perhaps in all police stations expect some detention facilities, but not only the specifics there can stand as this and about any specifics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As it stands. Yes, that's of course. Then that's about -- if it's the visit of Mr. Krajisnik. And the second issue, the second surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Given -- your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My submission with respect to the evidence of the visit of Mr. Mandic is that that's far more important and direct evidence, especially in light of the conversation between Krajisnik and Mandic, that would go to show knowledge on the part of the accused of the existence of a detention facility in which civilians who had been cleansed from the municipality were being held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Far less speculation about that, in fact, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- yes, I do understand. But would it then be mainly on the basis of his visit or on the basis of the telephone conversation intercepted or both or on what would the one add to the information contained in the other?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Corroborative of one another, Your Honour, aren't they? Especially when they're talking about contemporaneous time period. This is a -- it covers a time period in which the witness was in fact detained there. And they will be corroborated by other documentary and witness evidence that's going to form part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. As far as the order of -- I do understand for tomorrow another witness was scheduled. Of course, we have to decide first how to proceed with cross-examination, whether we would invite the Defence to start with that. I might say a few words about it at a later stage of this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll be playing one final intercepted conversation for Mr. Music, which has not been played before this Trial Chamber before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not contained on any of the CDs that have been presented into evidence? I see Ms. Javier nodding no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I understand we have yet to deliver the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But we'll be playing the audio, and you're in possession of the B/C/S and English-language transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the transcripts will get in the original language the addition A and the translation will be A.1. Perhaps we could already attribute a number to it, Mr. Registrar, that would be for the CD number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document will be then be referenced under reference P411, having indeed a translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Has a copy been given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. I think -- Mr. Usher, could you give the witness a B/C/S copy. Mr. Registrar, do you have any copies for us? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to play now a conversation dated July 1st, 1992, that purports to be between Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the transcript in front of you, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. If we could play the conversation now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Unidentified female: Hello. Sipcic: Good afternoon, gorgeous. Unidentified female: Good afternoon. Sipcic: Sipcic. Unidentified female: Excuse me? Sipcic: Colonel Sipcic. Unidentified female: Oh, good afternoon. How are you? Sipcic: I'm okay. Thank you. Unidentified female: I'm not used to this form of address, you know... Sipcic: Tell me, is your boss in? Unidentified female: Yes, the minister is in. Please, hold on, Colonel. Sipcic: Thank you. Momcilo Mandic: Hello. Sipcic: Hello, Mr. Minister. Momcilo Mandic: Hello, General. Sipcic: Where have you been? Momcilo Mandic: I'm right here. Yesterday I ... You weren't working. You weren't there? Sipcic: What do you mean I wasn't? Yesterday was worst day of my life. Momcilo Mandic: Either yesterday or the day before. It must have been yesterday you weren't there. Your fellow countryman would have known. Yes, yes. It was around 1200 hours. Sipcic: I was in the field. Will you stop by? Momcilo Mandic: I will. Sipcic: Here, the president wants to talk to you. Hello. Momcilo Mandic: Sure, I'll come by. When will you be free? Sipcic: I'll be here all the time. Momcilo Mandic: All right, I'll come when they are done. Sipcic: All right. Momcilo Mandic: Deal. Sipcic: Hold on, hold on. Momcilo Mandic: I'll see you. Radovan Karadzic: Hello. Momcilo Mandic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: Good afternoon. Momcilo Mandic: All the best, Mr. President. Radovan Karadzic: What's up Momo? Momcilo Mandic: Well, not much. I've just been to a government session and I'm here now. Radovan Karadzic: Uh-huh. Momcilo Mandic: We're working on an exchange now. We're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija. Radovan Karadzic: Oh, that's very important. Momcilo Mandic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: We'll immediately mobilise those fit for combat and the rest of them... Momcilo Mandic: Yes, yes, we're evacuating them. Radovan Karadzic: How many will there be? Momcilo Mandic: Well, I don't really know. We have many on the list. There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims, who have been kept here for seven days. No one's inquired about them, no one seems to care. I don't know what to do. Radovan Karadzic: Why don't --. Momcilo Mandic: No one's interested in them, these Muslims. Radovan Karadzic: Yeah. Momcilo Mandic: So we'll try to exchange them for these people from Hrasnica and ... Radovan Karadzic: Have you found that Croat in Kula for me? Momcilo Mandic: He's not there. Radovan Karadzic: Tomic. He must be in Kula. Momcilo Mandic: President, he's definitely not there. All the Croats are gone. There are no Croats in Kula. Radovan Karadzic: No, no. He was arrested early earlier. He's not in Dobrinja. Momcilo Mandic: President, all Croats have been exchanged. Here, let me check again and I'll call you back in five minutes. Radovan Karadzic: All right. If he's not there, let's then look for him somewhere else. Momcilo Mandic: Well, does the person who is asking about Tomic know where he was taken to, where he was picked up? Radovan Karadzic: There were three brothers. Two of them were released in Ilidza and the third one was kept in Ilidza and transferred to Kula. That's what happened. They were arrested in Ilidza. Momcilo Mandic: President, I'll call you back in five minutes. Radovan Karadzic: All right. Tell me, what was going on, what was I going to say. Do you know if Karlo's people have arrived down there? Momcilo Mandic: I don't know. Radovan Karadzic: That thing down there should be strengthened, all that ... Momcilo Mandic: Yes, yes, yes. I don't really know, because I just arrived from a government session ... Radovan Karadzic: That thing with the Greeks should be strengthened. Momcilo Mandic: Uh-huh. I really don't know. Radovan Karadzic: All right. Momcilo Mandic: Our Mico has left, hasn't he? Radovan Karadzic: Well, yes, but I don't know why he's -- after all. Momcilo Mandic: Well, I don't ... Radovan Karadzic: He's not suitable for this kind of thing. Momcilo Mandic: I don't get this thing, Mr. President. Radovan Karadzic: I mean, there we have, if we need to have someone up there to coordinate things we can. But we need someone to work permanently on the establishment of such a service. Momcilo Mandic: How long will you be there, President? Radovan Karadzic: I'll be here for a while. Momcilo Mandic: I was going to come there. Radovan Karadzic: I'll be here for a while. Momcilo Mandic: I'll be there in half an hour or so and I'll call you back in five or ten minutes. Radovan Karadzic: Deal. Momcilo Mandic: Have a good one. See you."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just note, I understood the procedure to be that we would have an indication of when the speakers change and we didn't have that. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what is usually done, especially since sometimes there were some -- there was some confusion about it. It not having been done, Ms. Loukas, if there would be any submission in relation to what part of the conversation is attributed to what person, then please let us know. Otherwise, we'll take it from the transcript that at least the change in interlocutors is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, you've clearly heard everything that was said in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us: As of July 1st, 1992, how many days had you been at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The 1st of July, from the 1st of July until the 21st of July. I spent only three nights in Lukavica and then they transferred us to Kula. But when they transferred us to Kula, we were in two rooms. That means that -- I mean, we who were separate. Rather those 47 were separated and we the rest of us --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, sorry. Let me perhaps be a little bit more clear when I ask you this question. In your statements which have been filed with the Trial Chamber, you've said that you were transferred to Kula from Lukavica after two or three days at Lukavica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Three nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So by the 1st of July, then, 1992, how many nights had you been at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I spent three nights in Lukavica, and then after that I was transferred to Kula. In Kula, they divided us up into two rooms, so it was overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, the question was not how many people there were, but by the 1st of July, how many days you had already spent in Kula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 25th we were transferred, so I was there five or six days. I already stated that on the 30th, they released 75 elderly prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, the question was just about how long you had been in Kula on the 1st of July. You have now answered that question. Ms. Edgerton please put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One last question. Were all the men with you during that time from Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. That concludes the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take any decision on whether to invite Ms. Loukas to start cross-examination at this moment, may I first inquire,

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your next witness, you would prefer to let him wait until whatever is still to be done in relation to this witness has been done or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis had better address that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis. Perhaps we could invite the witness to take his earphones off at this moment. Mr. Music, we are dealing with a procedural issue that might have some impact on your presence in this courtroom. May I invite you to take your earphones off for a while. Mr. Hannis. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you'll excuse me for a moment, Your Honour. I can go and speak with Mr. Tieger, who will be dealing with that next witness. I won't think it will take me more than three minutes to get down there and back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although of course you could have expected this situation to come up. So a bit of anticipation would -- but let's not lose any more time. If you would please try to get the answer to the question as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps it might be possible to take a short break and Ms. Edgerton can actually call Mr. Tieger on the phone that's in the courtroom and it might take a little bit less time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could have a short break, then. Would three minutes do, Ms. Edgerton? Yes. We'll then have a break for three or four minutes. --- Break taken at 1.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite the witness to take his earphones still off, because it's ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've spoken with Mr. Tieger, who in fact indicates that he's spoken with Mr. Stewart and there's -- Mr. Tieger is not aware at this moment of the location of the next witness. In fact, he could be travelling. He is travelling at this time. So they prefer to hold off and start tomorrow, and I think we'd prefer to finish with this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then it would need a recall of this witness, which is of course a waste of -- and of course what the Chamber is mainly concerned about is to what extent a cross-examination of the witness on the issues involved would contribute -- well, let's say would assist the Defence in lessening the probative value on those issues compared to the situation if the witness would not be cross-examined at all on these issues. Because, to be -- let me try to -- first of all, whatever is said at this moment always is situated in the moment, this very moment. That means that whatever the Chamber would give as its provisional impression would always be an impression that's based on what we've heard until now. And as far as the -- yes, Ms. Loukas. Well, to say that in many respects, and limited to the evidence we have heard on those occasions, I have to convey to the parties that the probative value of the examination-in-chief on these matters is, for various reasons, I would say almost non-existent. And therefore, of course, the Chamber wonders, and perhaps Ms. Loukas could express herself on that, whether the witness could not be cross-examined on the other parts and then whether there would really be a need to influence the provisional mind of the Chamber where, as it may be clear to the parties, it could more likely go in a wrong direction for the Defence than in a good direction for the Defence. Because there's hardly any direction to go there any more. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I go back to the point I made prior to the witness giving evidence this morning. I indicated that there were in fact two courses in my submission that the Trial Chamber might take. And that is, firstly, to exclude the evidence, in view of the recent nature of the evidence, in fact yesterday, after -- 12 years after the event and after four statements. But my point in relation to that, I think, Your Honour, has of course been strengthened by the nature of the way in which the witness gave his evidence and the additional surprise we were subject to later on. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, and looking at Rule 89(D), I would invite Your Honours -- 89(D), of course, stating a Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. Your Honour has indicated that the probative value of the evidence in relation to Mr. Krajisnik is at a near negligible level and in those circumstances, Your Honour, I would submit that the evidence should be excluded.
